rv.q: Laurence Connor and James Powell's rendition of Boublil and Schonberg's musical reinvention of Victor Hugo's novel is an absolute blinder.
Old-fashioned though it may seem in contrast, in its density and epic ambition, its mixture of high-powered ideas and gut-wrenching emotions, it’s a show that feels lastingly revolutionary.

We first meet the veteran producer Max Bialystock (Andy Nyman, scintillatingly seedy) flushing the reviews of his latest flop down the lavatory. Yet, swiftly segueing into a Fiddler on the Roof pastiche, he longs to be king of Broadway again. And he doesn’t care who he has to schtup and swindle to get there.
All in all, Les Mis and the refurbished Sondheim feel fit for purpose for the next decade or three.

But seeing Les Mis for a second time was a chastening experience and one that reminded me that there are two things that audiences crave in the theatre and that are all too rarely found: an optimistic philosophy and a direct appeal to the heart.
The show remains a thrilling triumph.

The surefire dud they settle on is a gooey paean to Hitler’s Third Reich, written by an ursine, helmet-wearing not-so-ex-Nazi (Harry Morrison), and directed by the explosively camp Roger de Bris (Trevor Ashley). What’s impressive about The Producers is just how sharp its teeth still are, nearly 60 years on.

I’d say Marber steers past them all quite deftly with his grimy, funny and well-judged production. Max certainly embodies more than a few tropes, but they’re exuberantly reclaimed by the triple whammy of Jewish writer, director and actor.
People love Les Mis with a passion and I can see why.

The production certainly outstays its welcome, especially during an 80-minute first half which director Patrick Marber fails to prevent from flagging at points. Nevertheless, when it comes to rehearsals for the show from hell, the sheer ridiculous over-the-top-ness is an ebullient joy that wins over even the hardest (feminist) hearts.

Given more room to breathe (and a bigger budget) at The Garrick, Patrick Marber's original lean and sparky production spreads its pidgeon wings and soars. We roared with delight throughout at the big numbers and broad gags, and the smaller, but no less joyous or clever, delights.
It's a must see and I'm not surprised it's still delighting audiences.
Much of the conversation around the incoming of the revamped Les Misérables production to the West End has revolved around the revolve - or lack thereof.
It barely needs to be said that the picture that [Les Miserables] paints of the poor echoes sights you can see in the streets every day, and so there is little point in denying its political punch.
Heavens, though, this is a fun evening. It starts preposterously well: two songs about our Broadway producer hero Max Bialystock (Andy Nyman), such a confirmed cynic he’s almost a romantic.
